body:
What makes a substance acidic or basic?

Many familiar substances have an acidic or basic character. Lemon juice and vinegar contain acids; soap solution and lime water are basic. Sour taste is a familiar property of many edible acids, while many bases are bitter and feel soapy. These are descriptive properties, not safe methods of identification: unknown chemicals must never be tasted or handled directly.

An acid produces hydrogen ions, represented as H+(aq), in water. These ions associate with water to form hydronium ions, H3O+. A base produces hydroxide ions, OH−, in aqueous solution.

For example, hydrochloric acid forms hydronium and chloride ions in water, whereas dissolved sodium hydroxide supplies sodium and hydroxide ions:

HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−

NaOH → Na+ + OH− (in water)

Natural acids and common bases

Substance or sourceImportant constituentCharacter
Lemon and orange juiceCitric acidAcidic
VinegarAcetic acidAcidic
CurdLactic acidAcidic
Tamarind and grapesTartaric acidAcidic
Ant stingMethanoic (formic) acidAcidic
Lime waterCalcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2Basic
Milk of magnesiaMagnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2Basic
Caustic sodaSodium hydroxide, NaOHBasic

Alkalis, ions and conductivity

An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are alkalis. Some bases are insoluble or only sparingly soluble, so every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.

Aqueous acid and alkali solutions conduct electricity because they contain mobile ions. By contrast, aqueous glucose and alcohol do not behave as acids merely because their molecules contain hydrogen: they do not release H+(aq) in the same way. Dry hydrogen chloride gas does not turn dry blue litmus red; moisture is needed to produce ions and show the characteristic acidic response.

Solution describes a uniform mixture; acidic and basic describe its chemical behaviour. A clear salt solution, an acid solution and a sugar solution can look alike but have different acid-base properties.

Prelims focus

  • Acids give H3O+ or H+(aq) in water; bases give OH−.
  • An alkali is a water-soluble base; an insoluble base is not an alkali.
  • Citric acid: citrus fruits; acetic acid: vinegar; lactic acid: curd.
  • Mobile ions explain why aqueous acid and alkali solutions conduct electricity.
  • Trap: A substance containing hydrogen need not be an acid.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 5, “Acids, Bases and Salts,” pp. 49–55; GCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4, pp. 38–44; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, sections 2.1 and 2.2, pp. 17–24 (consulted 3 November 2026).]

title: Acids, Bases and the Role of Water

body:
How indicators distinguish acidic and basic solutions

An acid-base indicator is a substance whose colour, or in certain cases odour, changes according to the acidic or basic nature of its surroundings. Its response is more reliable than guessing from taste or appearance. Different indicators have different characteristic responses; it is incorrect to assume that every indicator changes colour in both acid and base.

Indicator colour changes to remember

IndicatorAcidic solutionBasic solution
Litmus solutionRedBlue
Blue litmus paperTurns redStays blue
Red litmus paperStays redTurns blue
TurmericYellowReddish-brown
China rose extractDark pink or magentaGreen
PhenolphthaleinColourlessPink
Methyl orangeRedYellow

Litmus is a natural dye obtained from lichens. Neutral litmus solution is purple. Turmeric and China rose are also natural indicators; phenolphthalein and methyl orange are common synthetic indicators. In neutral water, turmeric remains yellow and phenolphthalein remains colourless. Methyl orange is yellow at neutral pH as well as in alkaline solutions; its red-to-yellow change occurs in an acidic pH range.

Interpreting the result correctly

When a liquid changes red litmus to blue, it is basic. When it changes blue litmus to red, it is acidic. If a blue strip stays blue, the liquid could be basic or neutral; this observation alone does not establish that it is basic. Similarly, unchanged red litmus could indicate an acidic or neutral liquid. A neutral solution ordinarily changes neither strip.

Some substances are olfactory indicators: their smell changes in acidic or basic surroundings. Onion, vanilla and clove are familiar school-level examples. A universal indicator is a mixture of indicators that gives a range of colours for different pH values, allowing a more detailed comparison than simple litmus.

A yellow turmeric stain may turn reddish-brown on contact with basic soap solution. This is a colour response of the indicator, not evidence that every reddish-brown substance is a base.

Prelims focus

  • Litmus comes from lichens; acidic litmus is red, basic litmus is blue.
  • Turmeric becomes reddish-brown in a basic medium.
  • China rose: dark pink in acid, green in base.
  • Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base.
  • Trap: Blue litmus remaining blue does not exclude a neutral solution.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 5, sections 5.1–5.3, pp. 49–54; GCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4, sections 4.1–4.3, pp. 38–43; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, section 2.1.1, pp. 17–19 (consulted 3 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Red turning blue proves basic; blue turning red proves acidic. Unchanged blue or red can also mean neutral, so either alone is inconclusive.
pictures.caption: Use the direction of each litmus colour change, not an unchanged colour alone.

title: Natural and Synthetic Acid-Base Indicators

body:
Acids reacting with metals

Many reactive metals displace hydrogen from dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas. For example:

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2

The gas is hydrogen, traditionally recognised by a characteristic pop with a flame. The general pattern is acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen. This does not apply to every metal-acid pair: copper, for example, does not release hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid. The behaviour also depends on the acid used.

Acids reacting with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates

Metal carbonates and metal hydrogencarbonates react with acids to give a salt, carbon dioxide and water. Compare the two equations:

Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2

NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2

Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms:

CO2 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3 + H2O

With excess carbon dioxide, the milkiness may disappear as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms. Thus, a carbonate gives CO2, whereas a typical reactive metal gives H2.

Neutralisation: acid plus base

In a neutralisation reaction, an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water, usually releasing heat. The school-level example is:

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O

At the ionic level, H+(aq) and OH−(aq) form water. If the appropriate amounts of a strong acid and a strong base are completely reacted, the resulting solution is approximately neutral. It is not correct to conclude that every salt solution is neutral: depending on the acid and base from which it is derived, a salt solution may be acidic, basic or neutral.

Oxides also show acid-base behaviour

Many metallic oxides are basic oxides and react with acids to form a salt and water. Copper(II) oxide illustrates this:

CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O

Many non-metallic oxides are acidic oxides. Carbon dioxide reacts with the base calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate and water, as shown above. These are useful patterns rather than statements about every oxide without exception.

Prelims focus

  • Acid + reactive metal: salt + H2.
  • Acid + carbonate or hydrogencarbonate: salt + CO2 + water.
  • CO2 makes lime water milky by forming CaCO3.
  • Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water, generally with heat release.
  • Metallic oxides are often basic; non-metallic oxides are often acidic.
  • Trap: Do not identify CO2 as the hydrogen released by a metal-acid reaction.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 5, sections 5.3–5.4, pp. 54–56; GCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4, sections 4.3–4.4, pp. 43–45; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, sections 2.1.2–2.1.6, pp. 19–22 (consulted 3 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Zinc with acid produces hydrogen that pops with a flame; sodium hydrogencarbonate with acid produces carbon dioxide that makes lime water milky.
pictures.caption: Metal and carbonate reactions can be distinguished by the gas produced.

title: Reactions of Acids, Bases and Their Salts

body:
Reading the pH scale

The pH of an aqueous solution indicates its acidic or basic character by reference to hydrogen-ion concentration. On the familiar school-level scale, values are generally shown from 0 to 14. At about 25°C, a neutral aqueous solution has pH 7; a value below 7 is acidic and a value above 7 is basic. Lower pH means a higher concentration of H+(aq) or H3O+.

The scale is not an ordinary linear scale. Under comparable conditions, a solution at pH 3 has approximately 10 times the hydrogen-ion concentration of one at pH 4. Everyday pH values are approximate: food composition, dilution and temperature can alter the measured value. The usual 0–14 range is convenient for school examples, not an absolute limit for every possible solution.

ExampleApproximate pHNature
Gastric juice1–2Strongly acidic
Lemon juiceAbout 2Acidic
Pure water at 25°C7Neutral
BloodAbout 7.4Slightly basic
Milk of magnesiaAbout 10Basic

Strong and weak are different from concentrated and dilute

A strong acid, such as hydrochloric acid, ionises extensively in water; a weak acid, such as acetic acid, ionises only partly. In contrast, concentrated and dilute describe how much acid or base is present in a given quantity of solution. A dilute strong acid is still a strong acid by its tendency to ionise. Adding water generally reduces an acid solution's hydrogen-ion concentration and raises its pH toward neutral. Concentrated acids and bases can release substantial heat when mixed with water and require trained handling.

Applications of pH and neutralisation

Digestive system and teeth

The stomach contains hydrochloric acid that helps digestion. Antacids, such as magnesium hydroxide in milk of magnesia, are mildly basic and can neutralise excess stomach acid. In the mouth, bacteria can produce acids from food residues. Enamel dissolution and tooth decay become more likely when mouth pH falls below about 5.5; cleaning teeth and using generally mildly basic toothpaste help counter this acid.

Rainwater and soil

Rainwater with pH below 5.6 is classified as acid rain. Acid-forming air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides contribute to it, and it can harm plants, water bodies and buildings. Crop plants require suitable soil pH conditions; acidic soil can be treated, where appropriate, with substances such as quicklime, CaO, or slaked lime, Ca(OH)2. Organic matter can help modify alkaline soil over time, but treatment depends on the soil and crop.

Prelims focus

  • pH < 7: acidic; pH = 7: neutral; pH > 7: basic, for ordinary aqueous solutions at about 25°C.
  • A difference of 1 pH unit corresponds to an approximately 10-fold difference in hydrogen-ion concentration.
  • Acid rain: rain with pH below 5.6.
  • Tooth enamel is more vulnerable when mouth pH falls below about 5.5.
  • Acidic soil may be corrected with CaO or Ca(OH)2.
  • Trap: Strong and concentrated do not mean the same thing.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, section 2.3 and Figure 2.7, pp. 25–28 (consulted 3 November 2026); NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 5, section 5.4, pp. 55–56; GCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4, pp. 44–45.]
